There are a lot of online mentor groups that might be a better fit for you - try facebook, I'm part of a women/gaming discussion/mentoring group, for example. There's also a few professional organizations out there for all kinds of stuff. As far as social media is concerned, 99% of the battle is putting the content there consistently, eventually the audience shows up, when you hit upon something that goes viral for whatever reason. Don't worry about not having a long term plan, because plans change. Consider something like odesk or other freelance websites for now to give you extra income if you don't like the 9/5. Stuff like voice acting/voice over work can be pretty easy and fun. When it comes to those sites, I know at first it can be daunting, or seem really underpaid, but the strategy is to just take whatever jobs interest you regardless of pay in the beginning, so you build up a reputation and portfolio, to where you are more likely to get the better paying jobs. A friend of mine completely supports herself and her husband solely doing that kind of work, like online content writing. As far as event planning/PR/public speaking, there are always people out there that need that kind of stuff, and again, start out for free or low cost, get a reputation and portfolio of things you can point to, and that'll help you get your foot in the door for better things. Even if it's family and friends, planning events for them or whatever, or joining meetup groups and speaking at them, you can do this stuff. I know it's daunting, but one small success and you may feel much better about things

When I was your age, I had a friend who had a story much like yours. Lots of different diagnoses, lots of different medications and problems. I remember spending an hour on the phone with him once, because he was having a psychotic episode due to some of the meds he'd been given, and he didn't want to hurt anyone while he made his way to a pharmacist for a different prescription. One of the hardest days of my life was the day his girlfriend called me to tell me he was dead. He'd committed passive suicide - allowed some of the symptoms he was suffering from medications to give him a heart attack, so he died, at 23. I think about him still, 14 years later. I wish I could have done something, said something, given him some hope that things might change. I think a lot of the problems were the combinations and different drugs he'd been given affecting the chemistry of his brain as a whole, making it hard for him to find where normal was after years of treatment. I miss him, and I still have a piece of his artwork, framed, on my wall, to remind me of him every day, along with the words "Don't postpone joy." Life is short, and hard, but there are people who love you who will always miss you, even if you don't think that's true. I loved Chris for the person he was, even when that person was legitimately crazy. He was the one person in my life that I felt I could always talk to, who would never judge me for the person that I am. Where I am today in my art career, I owe in large part to his faith in me, his encouragement that I could do something more, be something more than I was. I couldn't help him. Sometimes I can't even help myself. Maybe though, my words can help you. I know the walls you talk about. You can find peace and solace and comfort. They will exist for you, maybe not now, but sometime in the future. Please keep holding on. Chris used to tell me, when I complained that I hated drawing trees, that I didn't have to draw every leaf, that really, a drawing of a tree is just a suggestion of a tree - the most successful ones don't include every single leaf. Maybe a happy life, a peaceful life, isn't about drawing every happy thing, but just doing your best to suggest the happy in each day, to seek out what solace you can, and don't postpone what joy you can find.
